big: AMFI publishes industry data around the 10th of each month. A client who hears one fresh fact tied to her own SIP remembers the meeting. A client who sits through twenty slides remembers the clock.

lines: I do not follow the news. Why should I care that SIPs hit a record in August?
Because of what it says about people like you. The skill is to link the fact to her situation within thirty seconds.

alt: Five bars of monthly SIP inflows in thousand crore rupees from August 2025 to August 2026
caps: Monthly SIP money in ₹ thousand crore, from AMFI. The months are picked, not consecutive.
February 2026: ₹29,845 crore. March, in the fall: ₹32,087 crore, a record then.
July: ₹31,961 crore. August 2026: ₹32,297 crore, a new record.
A fresh fact, 14% above a year earlier. Now link it to the client.
small: August 2026, up 14% on a year earlier

h: Two ways to use the same data
alt: Two bars splitting a thirty minute meeting into time on slides, client talk and decisions
caps: Two versions of one 30-minute meeting. In the first, a 20-slide deck takes 20 minutes.
The client speaks for 3 minutes and leaves with few decisions.
In the second, one fresh fact and its link take about 2 minutes. Then she talks.
Data earns its place by starting the talk about her money, not by filling the time.

intro: AMFI figures for August 2026. The ratio compares one month's closures with that month's new SIPs.
note: Closures include SIPs that simply reached their end date. The ratio does not mean that 81% of investors quit.

q: It is the 12th and AMFI's August data is out. Which opener suits a client whose ₹15,000 SIP is three years old?
opts: AUM is ₹87.08 lakh crore, and SIP assets are ₹18.62 lakh crore
A record ₹32,297 crore came via SIPs in August. Same goal?
Let me start with a 20-slide deck on the industry this month
The market looks stretched, so you may want to pause this month
why: Two big numbers with no link to her give her nothing to answer. A statistic needs a bridge to her own SIP.
One fresh fact, linked to her SIP, ends in a question about her goal. That turns the data into a conversation about her.
A long deck uses the meeting for slides, not for her. The client speaks last, if at all, and decisions get squeezed.
Pausing is advice with no reason behind it. A data point should open a talk, not hand her a call to stop a three-year SIP.

q: A client reads that 81% of SIPs stop and wants to stop his. In August 2026, 53.82 lakh SIPs closed or matured against 66.39 lakh new ones. What is the best reply?
opts: He is right; four in five SIPs fail, so stopping is normal
The figure is invented, since AMFI publishes no SIP data
It counts only equity SIPs, so it does not apply to his fund
It sets one month's closures against new SIPs, not all SIPs
why: The ratio does not say four in five SIPs fail. About 5% of the 10.02 crore contributing accounts closed that month.
AMFI does publish SIP data monthly, including registrations and closures. The 81.1% comes from those figures.
The figure covers SIPs overall, not only equity ones, so that is not why it fails to apply to him.
53.82 divided by 66.39 is 81.1%. It sets closures, including SIPs that ended on schedule, against one month's new SIPs.

q: Your one-page sheet shows July's figures. It is mid-September and AMFI's August data is out. A client asks for the latest SIP flows. What do you do?
opts: Refresh from AMFI's August data and quote it with its month
Quote July's figure as the latest, since it is only a month old
Quote a news site's figure, whichever you saw last
Say you will update the sheet when the quarter ends
why: AMFI releases monthly data around the 10th. Refreshing then, and naming the month, keeps you accurate and credible.
July's figure is not the latest once August's is out. Quoting it as current is a stale fact that a client may check.
Pick a source and stick to it. The last site you saw may be late or may carry a slip, and the client cannot trace it.
A quarterly update is too slow for monthly data. By then the sheet would be a full three months out of date.

q: Two reports show March 2026 net equity inflows as ₹40,366 crore and ₹40,450 crore. A client asks which is right. What is the best practice?
opts: Quote the average of the two, to stay on the safe side
Quote the larger one, as it sounds more convincing
Quote AMFI's own release with its source and month
Avoid quoting numbers altogether, to prevent any slip
why: An average of two reports is a figure nobody published. It adds an error of its own, and you cannot source it.
Choosing the figure that sounds better is persuasion, not accuracy, and a client who checks will doubt your other numbers.
The primary source settles it, and the month lets the client check. Secondary reports can slip, so go back to AMFI.
Numbers are what make your point credible. Avoiding them leaves you with opinions, and the client with nothing to weigh.

pts: Open with one fresh fact, such as a record ₹32,297 crore of SIPs in August 2026, and link it to the client's situation within 30 seconds.
Carry a one-page sheet: AUM, SIPs, defence, gold, rates. Refresh it every month after AMFI's data, around the 10th.
Name the source and the month, and read a ratio like the 81% stoppage ratio before you quote it.
